passage:
Thursday, 9 pm

Dear diary, last night I got in bed at ten thinking I'd just check one video. Then the group was sharing clips from Sunaina's party and I didn't want to be the one who missed the joke tomorrow. Then another video. Then a cooking one, I don't even cook.
My eyes were burning but my brain was wide awake.
Looked up and it was nearly two.
Today I was a zombie. Snapped at Sunaina when she only asked if I'd done the chemistry sheet. She looked hurt.
Tonight the phone is going on my desk across the room. The group chat will survive without me.

Shreya

qa.q: What time was it when Shreya looked up?
qa.a: It was nearly two.

qa.q: Why did Shreya keep watching even with burning eyes?
qa.a: Shreya was afraid of missing out on the party clips and the joke the next day, and the videos kept Shreya's mind wide awake.

qa.q: What is Shreya's plan for tonight, and why might it work?
qa.a: Putting the phone on the desk across the room means Shreya cannot keep reaching for one more video in bed.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when Shreya snapped?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt hurt and confused, since she only asked about the chemistry sheet.

grounding: It shows a teenager believing one more video is harmless, with fear of missing out keeping the diarist up, and mood dropping the next day.

'Indu, you've buttered the same toast three times.'
'I'm tired, Mumma.'
'What time did you sleep?'
Indu shrugged. 'Two? Maybe later.'
'Were you on your phone?'
'Just a few videos. And the group chat. Everyone was talking about the concert. If I don't reply, they'll make plans without me.'
Urmila sat down. 'And now?'
'Now I feel horrible. My head hurts and I snapped at Vir on the stairs.'
'One more video never feels like much, does it?'
'It's like my brain won't turn off.'
'What if the phone charges in the kitchen from eleven? Your friends will still be there tomorrow.'
Indu sighed. 'Can I try it on weeknights first?'
'Deal.'

qa.a: Indu was afraid of missing out on plans in the group chat about the concert.

qa.a: Charging the phone in the kitchen from eleven, so the light and chat stop keeping Indu's mind awake.

qa.q: How might Vir have felt when Indu snapped on the stairs?
qa.a: Vir was probably hurt or confused, not knowing Indu was running on little sleep.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose 'one more video' and fear of missing out delay sleep and sour the next day's mood, and a plan to charge the phone outside the bedroom.

passage: Last spring, I was getting maybe five hours of sleep a night, and I didn't understand why I felt so awful. I'm Sabina. My routine was: into bed at eleven, phone in hand, 'just one video'. Then another. Then friends' stories, and the fear I'd miss something important. By one I'd feel tired, but my brain was lit up like the screen. Mornings, I was foggy and weepy and yelled at my brother Karthik for breathing too loud. Karthik was the one who dared me: 'Leave your phone with me for one week.' I bought a cheap alarm clock and did it. The first two nights were awful, just lying there. By the fourth, I was asleep by eleven-thirty. And I didn't miss anything that mattered.

qa.q: What did Sabina buy for the experiment?
qa.a: A cheap alarm clock.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel in the mornings when scrolling late?
qa.a: Sabina felt foggy, weepy and irritable, snapping at Karthik.

qa.q: What did Karthik's dare show about the phone in bed?
qa.a: That without it, sleep came earlier and nothing important was missed, even if the first nights were hard.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt being yelled at in the mornings?
qa.a: Karthik was probably annoyed and hurt, which may be why he offered the dare.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose scrolling in bed, fear of missing out and bright light delay sleep and lower mood, and how putting the phone away helps.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Wednesday
Ankita, sixteen, came in today saying she feels 'sad for no reason' and can't concentrate. When we talked through her evenings, she said she scrolls in bed until one or two most nights, watching friends' reels and feeling she's the only one not having fun. She knows it makes her tired but says, 'One more video doesn't feel like anything.' We talked about how bright light and worry about missing out keep the mind awake long after the body is tired. She agreed to a two-week experiment: phone charging in the living room from ten-thirty, and a book instead. We'll check in next Wednesday, and I've asked her permission to share the plan with her mother, which she gave.
Simran

qa.q: What does Ankita watch when scrolling in bed?
qa.a: Friends' reels.

qa.q: How does Ankita feel when watching friends' reels at night?
qa.a: She feels sad and left out, as if she is the only one not having fun.

qa.q: What experiment did Ankita agree to?
qa.a: Charging her phone in the living room from ten-thirty and reading a book instead for two weeks.

qa.q: How might Ankita's mother feel hearing about the plan?
qa.a: She may feel relieved that Ankita is getting support and glad to be included.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose late-night scrolling, fear of missing out and bright light delay sleep and lower mood, and a counsellor's gentle plan to move the phone away.
